Three variants of a new Ni-based superalloy (Alloy1, Alloy2, Alloy3) were studied and compared to the benchmark CM247LC alloy.
The new alloy compositions were designed using the Alloys-by-Design (ABD) method to optimize processability, creep resistance, oxidation resistance, and other properties.
The new alloy compositions had equal equilibrium γ' volume fraction at 900°C but varying (Nb+Ta)/Al ratios.
Laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) was used to additively manufacture the alloy samples, with a laser power of 200W, layer thickness of 30 μm, and scan speed of 0.875 m/s.
Optical microscopy and X-ray computed tomography (XCT) revealed that the new alloys printed with no evidence of cracks, while CM247LC exhibited crack-like defects.
All compositions showed some gas-related porosity, particularly at thin wall sections like the turbine blade trailing edge.
Atom probe tomography (APT) showed that the Nb and Ta concentrations in the γ' of Alloy3 were approximately twice as high as in Alloy1.
A novel sub-solvus heat treatment (HT3) was proposed for the new alloys, avoiding the embrittlement seen with super-solvus heat treatment.
Alloy3, with the highest (Nb+Ta) content, exhibited the greatest flow stress up to 900°C, exceeding that of CM247LC.
The creep resistance of CM247LC was superior to the new alloy variants, likely due to CM247LC's greater γ' volume fraction and higher C and B contents.
Oxidation-assisted cracking (OAC) testing was performed to assess the influence of oxidation on crack growth.
The median particle size (D50) of the alloy powders used for additive manufacturing was between 32.3 and 33.0 μm.
The new alloy compositions were designed using the Alloys-by-Design (ABD) method to optimize multiple properties.
The sub-solvus HT3 heat treatment exhibited greater high-temperature ductility compared to the super-solvus HT1 treatment.
The directionality of cracks in CM247LC, parallel to the build direction, helped maintain its creep resistance despite the processing-induced defects.
